individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces InfoDet, a large-scale dataset for detecting charts and human-recognizable objects (HROs) in infographics, containing 11,264 real and 90,000 synthetic infographics with over 14 million bounding box annotations. Annotations are produced via programmatic parsing for synthetic data and a model-in-the-loop human-refined approach for real data. The paper demonstrates three applications: a Thinking-with-Boxes grounded chain-of-thought prompting scheme that improves VLM performance on ChartQAPro, an evaluation of 11 object detection models on InfoDet, and transfer learning to document layout and UI detection (Rico, DocGenome).
Strengths: Large-scale dataset with 101,264 infographics and 14M+ annotations, filling a gap in infographic element detection; combines real and synthetic data for diversity and scale.
Model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline reduces manual effort while achieving high precision/recall (93.9%/96.7%) and is a practical contribution for dataset construction.
The Thinking-with-Boxes scheme provides a clear application: grounding VLMs with detected elements improves chart understanding on ChartQAPro across multiple models.
Comprehensive evaluation of 11 object detection models, showing InfoDet is necessary for infographic element detection and useful for fine-tuning.
Demonstrates generalization to document layout and UI detection, supporting broader utility.
Includes diversity, bias, and quality analyses of the dataset, and a clear ethics statement regarding data licenses.
Weaknesses: Real-infographic annotations are model-generated and human-corrected, but the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement or per-category annotation quality; the reported precision/recall is only on a random 1,250-sample subset.

Mark-level annotations (26 sub-element categories) appear to be available only for synthetic infographics; real infographics lack fine-grained chart sub-type labels, which may limit mark-level model evaluation and generalization.

The Thinking-with-Boxes gains are modest (e.g., +1.7 for o4-mini overall) and only evaluated on ChartQAPro; no comparison against other visual grounding methods (e.g., Set-of-Marks) or other chart QA benchmarks.

The evaluation of foundation models is incomplete: T-Rex2 and DINO-X are only tested with 4-shot prompting due to API costs, and some models are not fine-tuned due to memory constraints, making the comparison less systematic.
Text annotations are obtained with PP-OCRv4 without any reported accuracy on infographic text, which could affect both the dataset quality and the grounded CoT prompts.

Dataset construction may introduce bias: real infographics are from only 10 platforms, and synthetic data derive from 1,072 templates; the 92.64% CLIP coverage still leaves a non-trivial fraction of real infographics unrepresented.
Questions: How were the 1,250 evaluation samples selected for annotation quality, and what was the inter-annotator agreement among the experts?

Are mark-level annotations available for real infographics or only for synthetic ones? If only synthetic, how does that affect the mark-level detection evaluation and the claim of comprehensive annotation?
What is the accuracy of PP-OCRv4 text annotations on infographics, and how does OCR noise affect the grounded CoT prompting results?
Why did few-shot prompting not improve T-Rex2/DINO-X beyond 4-shot? Would more examples or different prompt designs change the conclusions?
How does Thinking-with-Boxes compare with other visual prompting methods such as Set-of-Marks or SAM-based grounding, especially on plain charts?
The enhanced relaxed accuracy metric was modified (e.g., removing punctuation/units). Were these modifications applied consistently to all baselines, and could they affect the reported improvements?

What is the degree of overlap between synthetic template chart types and those found in real infographics? Does the 92.64% CLIP coverage imply that 7.36% of real infographics have no synthetic counterpart, and how does that affect model performance on those rare types?
Have the authors verified that the sources for synthetic data (IconQA images, VizNet tables, GPT-4o mini generated text) have licenses compatible with releasing the derived dataset?
Limitations: Real infographics are collected from only 10 online platforms, which may not cover the full diversity of infographic designs.
Annotation quality of real data depends on model-in-the-loop and human review, but no inter-annotator agreement or per-category accuracy is reported.
Mark-level annotations are primarily derived from synthetic data, limiting fine-grained evaluation on real infographics.
Text annotations via PP-OCRv4 may contain errors, especially on stylized or overlapping text in infographics.
Chart understanding evaluation is limited to ChartQAPro; performance on other chart QA benchmarks (e.g., ChartQA, PlotQA, InfographicVQA) is not shown.
The object detection model used to annotate real data was trained on synthetic data, potentially introducing a circular bias when the same model is later evaluated on InfoDet.
The dataset release links to source URLs rather than hosting images, which may affect reproducibility if sources become unavailable.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces InfoDet, a large-scale dataset for detecting charts and human-recognizable objects (HROs) in infographics. It contains 11,264 real and 90,000 synthetic infographics with over 14 million bounding box annotations. Annotations are created via programmatic methods for synthetic images and model-in-the-loop with expert refinement for real images. The authors demonstrate the dataset's utility through three applications: improving VLM chart understanding with a Thinking-with-Boxes grounded chain-of-thought scheme, benchmarking object detection models, and applying the model to document layout and UI element detection.
Strengths: Large-scale dataset with 101,264 infographics and over 14M bounding boxes, addressing a gap in infographic element detection.
Combines programmatic and model-in-the-loop annotation, which reduces human labor and enables scaling.
Provides multiple applications showing potential utility for chart understanding, detection model evaluation, and layout detection.
Includes diversity and bias analyses and addresses ethical considerations for data collection.
Weaknesses: The annotation quality is validated on only 1,250 images using precision/recall without specifying IoU thresholds, and the comparison to COCO/Objects365 is not apples-to-apples.
The Thinking-with-Boxes improvement on ChartQAPro is modest (e.g., o4-mini +1.7 overall), and no oracle or detection-error analysis is provided to isolate the benefit.
Real infographic annotations rely on a model trained on synthetic data, which may introduce domain bias; expert correction details are not fully described.
Experimental evaluation is limited: only three closed-source VLMs are tested, and detection model comparisons in the main text are incomplete.
Dataset and code links are redacted, preventing verification of data quality and reproducibility.
The annotation categories are coarse (e.g., HROs are only two classes), and fine-grained classification for real images is deferred.
Questions: How were the 1,250 images selected for annotation quality evaluation, and what IoU threshold was used for precision/recall?
What is the upper-bound performance of Thinking-with-Boxes with ground-truth boxes, and how much do detection errors degrade the results?
How many experts participated in annotation refinement, and what was the inter-annotator agreement?
What exact instructions were given to GPT-4o mini for filtering and text generation, and what quality checks were applied?
Are the dataset and code publicly available, and what are the exact licenses for the real infographics and derived annotations?
Why does o3 show a higher instruction-following error rate, and could this be mitigated by different prompting or evaluation strategies?
Limitations: The dataset is biased toward the selected 10 online platforms and the 1,072 synthetic templates, which may not cover all infographic styles.
The synthetic distribution may not fully match the real-world domain, and only 92.64% coverage in CLIP feature space is shown.
The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline may propagate errors from the initial synthetic-trained model into real annotations.
The chart understanding experiments are limited to ChartQAPro and three proprietary VLMs, so generalization to other benchmarks is unclear.
The dataset is not currently verifiable due to redacted links in the anonymized submission.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper introduces InfoDet, a large-scale dataset for detecting charts and human-recognizable objects (HROs) in infographics, containing 11,264 real and 90,000 synthetic infographics with over 14 million bounding-box annotations. Annotations are produced by programmatic extraction for synthetic images and a model-in-the-loop process with iterative expert refinement for real images. The authors demonstrate the dataset through three applications: a Thinking-with-Boxes scheme using grounded chain-of-thought prompting that improves VLM performance on ChartQAPro, a benchmark of object detection models, and transfer of the trained detector to document layout and UI-element detection.
Strengths: The dataset is large-scale (101,264 infographics, 14M+ boxes) and fills a clear gap in infographic element detection, which prior datasets either ignore or only cover at very small scale.

The combination of real and synthetic infographics with complementary annotation strategies (programmatic for synthetic, model-in-the-loop with expert refinement for real) is practical and well-motivated.

The three applications are useful: the Thinking-with-Boxes scheme improves VLM chart understanding on ChartQAPro, the detector benchmark compares a broad set of models, and the transfer experiments to Rico and DocGenome demonstrate generalizability.
The paper includes useful analyses of diversity, bias, synthetic fidelity, and cross-dataset generalization, which strengthen the credibility of the resource.
The authors address legal/ethical aspects of data collection by releasing only source URLs and checking platform policies, and they describe filtering for harmful or sensitive content.
Weaknesses: The quality of real-infographic annotations is only evaluated on a sample of 1,250 images; the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, the number of annotators, or a detailed annotation protocol, leaving uncertainty about annotation consistency and quality.

Fine-grained annotations (75 chart types and 26 mark-level categories) are only available for synthetic infographics; real infographics lack these fine-grained labels due to low GPT-4o classification accuracy, limiting the dataset's usefulness for fine-grained real-world detection.

There are presentation inconsistencies, such as Table 4's caption calling it 'element level' while the text describes it as 'mark level,' and the mAP metric is not clearly defined for a two-class element-level task.

VLM experiments rely on proprietary models (o1/o3/o4-mini) and show only modest gains (e.g., overall accuracy from 63.2 to 64.9 for o4-mini); no open-source VLM is tested, and the effect of detection/OCR errors on the grounded CoT pipeline is not analyzed.

The object detection benchmark is somewhat limited: foundation models are mostly evaluated zero-shot with two fixed class names, few-shot prompting is only tested on MQ-GLIP and T-Rex2, and standard fine-tuning is restricted by GPU memory, making the comparison less comprehensive than claimed.
Questions: How many expert annotators were involved in the model-in-the-loop refinement, what instructions were they given, and what is the inter-annotator agreement or a more detailed quality assessment on real infographics?

Are the 75 chart-type labels and 26 mark-level labels available only for synthetic infographics? If so, how can a model be trained or evaluated for fine-grained chart-type and mark-level detection on real infographics?

In the Thinking-with-Boxes scheme, what is the individual contribution of the OCR text versus the detected bounding boxes? Was there an ablation with only OCR text or only boxes to quantify the effect of detection errors?

How were the 1,072 design templates derived from real infographics? Are they shared with ChartGalaxy, and what safeguards prevent synthetic infographics from being overly biased toward these templates?
What is the exact license of the InfoDet dataset itself, and are the synthetic infographics released as images or only as source URLs?
Limitations: The quality of real-infographic annotations is verified on only 1,250 sampled images, with no inter-annotator agreement reported, which leaves the reliability of the full annotation set uncertain.
Fine-grained chart-type and mark-level annotations are absent for real infographics, reducing the dataset's coverage of real-world fine-grained detection tasks.
The dataset primarily comes from English-language or globally oriented platforms, so it may underrepresent non-English infographics and diverse regional design styles.

The model-in-the-loop annotation process may propagate biases from the initial InternImage model trained on synthetic data into the real-infographic labels, and such systematic bias is not thoroughly measured.
The VLM evaluation is limited to proprietary models and ChartQAPro; it is unclear whether the Thinking-with-Boxes gains transfer to open-source VLMs or other chart-understanding benchmarks.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces InfoDet, a large-scale dataset for detecting charts and human-recognizable objects (HROs) in infographics. It contains 11,264 real and 90,000 synthetic infographics with over 14 million bounding box annotations, constructed via programmatic annotation for synthetic images and a model-in-the-loop pipeline with expert refinement for real images. The authors demonstrate three applications: a Thinking-with-Boxes grounded chain-of-thought prompting method that improves VLM performance on ChartQAPro, a benchmark evaluation of 11 object detection models, and transfer of the trained model to document layout and UI element detection.
Strengths: InfoDet fills a clear gap by providing a large-scale, diverse dataset for infographic element detection, combining real and synthetic data with fine-grained annotations for texts, charts, HROs, and sub-elements.
The model-in-the-loop annotation approach is practical and reduces human effort, with reported precision and recall comparable to established detection datasets.

The paper provides a thorough evaluation of many detection models and adaptation methods, showing that foundation models struggle on infographics while fine-tuning on InfoDet yields strong performance.
The demonstration of transfer to document layout and UI detection (Rico, DocGenome) suggests InfoDet is a useful pre-training resource beyond infographics.
The dataset analysis covers diversity, bias, and synthetic fidelity, which adds credibility to the resource.
Weaknesses: The improvements from Thinking-with-Boxes are modest (e.g., o4-mini overall 63.2 to 64.9) and no statistical significance tests are reported; the modified evaluation metric (punctuation/unit/ratio normalization) lacks sensitivity analysis and may affect comparability with ChartQAPro.

The construction of real annotations is underspecified: the number of expert annotators, number of refinement rounds, inter-annotator agreement, and whether the final detection model is retrained on corrected real labels are not clearly stated.

Mark-level annotations appear to be generated only for synthetic infographics, but mark-level evaluation is performed on the InfoDet test set without clarifying how real images (which lack such annotations) are handled.
There are internal inconsistencies, such as 75 chart types listed in the appendix versus 67 chart types reported in the diversity analysis.

Releasing only URLs for real infographics may hinder reproducibility if links change or content is removed, and the paper does not compare InfoDet against prior detection-specific infographic benchmarks.
Questions: How many expert annotators were involved, how many refinement rounds were conducted, and what was the inter-annotator agreement during real annotation?
Was the final InternImage-based model fine-tuned on the expert-corrected real annotations or only on synthetic data?
How are mark-level annotations handled for real infographics in the test set during mark-level evaluation?
Why does the diversity analysis report 67 chart types while the annotation taxonomy lists 75, and are all 75 present in the dataset?
Would the reported ChartQAPro improvements hold under the official metric without the three modifications to enhanced relaxed accuracy?
Could the zero-/few-shot prompting results for foundation models be sensitive to the specific class names 'chart' and 'human recognizable object'? Were alternative prompts explored?
Limitations: The real infographics are collected from only 10 platforms, which may introduce domain bias.
Synthetic infographics are generated from templates derived from real infographics, potentially limiting coverage of novel designs.
Real annotations are model-generated and expert-corrected, so residual errors may remain despite quality checks.
Mark-level annotations are not available for real infographics, limiting the scope of fine-grained evaluation.
Releasing only source URLs rather than images may lead to broken links or non-reproducible downloads.
The paper does not provide a protocol for using InfoDet as a benchmark, making comparisons across future methods less standardized.

review.Summary: The paper introduces InfoDet, a large-scale dataset for detecting charts and human-recognizable objects (HROs) in infographics. It contains 11,264 real and 90,000 synthetic infographics with over 14 million bounding boxes for texts, charts, HROs, and fine-grained sub-elements. The authors combine programmatic annotation for synthetic images and a model-in-the-loop process with expert refinement for real images. They demonstrate three applications: a Thinking-with-Boxes prompting scheme that improves VLM performance on ChartQAPro, benchmarking of 11 object detection models showing fine-tuning on InfoDet outperforms zero-/few-shot prompting, and transfer learning to document layout and UI detection tasks. They also release the dataset and model for research.
Strengths: InfoDet fills a clear gap: existing chart datasets are either plain-chart oriented or too small (e.g., Borkin et al. has only 393 images) for training robust detection models.
The combination of real and synthetic infographics (101,264 total) with 14M+ bounding boxes is a substantial resource for infographic element detection.
The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline with expert refinement achieves reported precision (93.9%) and recall (96.7%) comparable to high-quality datasets like COCO and Objects365.
The Thinking-with-Boxes scheme consistently improves ChartQAPro over direct, CoT, and PoT baselines across three state-of-the-art VLMs (o1, o3, o4-mini).
The paper provides a broad evaluation of 11 detection models, revealing that zero-/few-shot prompting is insufficient for infographics and that fine-tuning on InfoDet yields strong gains.
Transfer learning experiments on Rico and DocGenome show InfoDet is beneficial as additional pretraining data for graphic layout detection.
Ethical considerations are addressed by filtering harmful content and releasing only source URLs instead of redistributing third-party images.
Weaknesses: The paper's presentation is significantly hindered by incomplete tables and broken internal references (e.g., Table 2 shows only one row but the text describes multiple ablation sub-tables; several result tables are truncated). This makes it difficult to verify the reported claims.

The annotation quality evaluation is not fully described: it lacks details on the number of experts, inter-annotator agreement, and whether the reported precision/recall is measured on the auto-generated or final corrected annotations.

The Thinking-with-Boxes gains are modest (e.g., o4-mini overall from 63.2 to 64.9) and no statistical significance tests are provided; there is also no comparison to using ground-truth boxes to measure the impact of detection errors.

Zero-shot detection models are prompted with vague class names 'chart' and 'human recognizable object', which may understate their capabilities; more specific prompts or few-shot examples with diverse visual descriptions could yield fairer comparisons.

Fine-grained subcategory annotations (75 chart types, 26 mark types) exist only for synthetic images; real infographics lack these due to model limitations, restricting the dataset's utility for tasks requiring detailed element understanding.

The transfer learning experiments show only modest gains when InfoDet is added to a strong pretraining combination (e.g., Rico from 51.8 to 53.6, DocGenome from 78.7 to 80.0), raising questions about its incremental value beyond existing large-scale resources.
Questions: How was the annotation quality evaluation conducted? Were the 1,250 sampled infographics evaluated before or after the expert refinement rounds, and what exact protocol did the experts follow?

In the Thinking-with-Boxes experiments, what is the performance when using ground-truth bounding boxes instead of the predicted boxes? This would isolate the effect of detection accuracy on chart understanding.

Could the improvements from grounded CoT be partly due to the added textual descriptions of elements? The ablation shows visual-only and text-only both underperform the combined, but is there a condition with only original image plus textual descriptions (without boxes)?
For zero-shot detection, would more descriptive prompts (e.g., listing chart types like 'bar chart', 'pie chart') improve the performance of models like DINO-X and Grounding DINO?
What is the inter-annotator agreement or variance among expert annotators in the model-in-the-loop process?
The paper mentions that models trained on InfoDet transfer better to VG-DCU than vice versa, but only on four common categories. Is this a fair evaluation of generalizability?

Are the synthetic infographics sufficiently diverse in terms of chart types, layouts, and HROs? The paper reports 92.64% coverage of real infographics in CLIP/UMAP space, but was there a human evaluation of the synthetic-to-real gap beyond 500 samples?
Limitations: Real infographics lack fine-grained chart/HRO subcategory annotations due to the limited accuracy of GPT-4o classification (61.49% for charts, 74.69% for HROs), meaning the detailed categories are only available for synthetic data.
The dataset is sourced from 10 online platforms, which may introduce selection bias toward specific styles, topics, or geographical regions.
Text annotations for real infographics are obtained from an OCR model (PP-OCRv4) and may contain errors, particularly in stylized or overlapping text.
The Thinking-with-Boxes method relies on a specialized detector; its effectiveness on unseen infographic styles or domains is not extensively tested.
The synthetic data generation is template-based, which may not fully capture the complexity and composite charts found in real-world infographics, as acknowledged by the authors.
The paper does not provide a scaling analysis showing how detection performance improves with the size of InfoDet, which would help justify the 90,000 synthetic images.

review.Summary: The paper introduces InfoDet, a large-scale dataset for detecting charts and human-recognizable objects (HROs) in infographics, containing 11,264 real and 90,000 synthetic infographics with over 14 million bounding-box annotations. Annotations are generated via programmatic parsing for synthetic data and a model-in-the-loop with expert refinement for real data. The paper demonstrates three applications: a Thinking-with-Boxes grounded chain-of-thought prompting scheme that improves VLM performance on ChartQAPro, an evaluation of 11 object detection models on InfoDet, and transfer learning to document layout and UI detection (Rico, DocGenome).
Strengths: InfoDet fills a clear gap in infographic element detection, providing a large-scale resource (101,264 infographics, 14M+ boxes) that combines real and synthetic data for diversity and scale.
The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline is practical and reduces human effort while achieving reported precision/recall (93.9%/96.7%) comparable to established detection datasets.
The Thinking-with-Boxes scheme consistently improves ChartQAPro performance over strong baselines across several state-of-the-art VLMs, demonstrating a useful application for chart understanding.
The benchmark of 11 object detection models reveals that zero-/few-shot prompting is insufficient for infographics and that fine-tuning on InfoDet yields strong gains, providing a valuable reference.
Transfer learning to document layout and UI detection (Rico, DocGenome) suggests InfoDet is a useful pretraining resource beyond infographics.
The paper includes analyses of diversity, bias, synthetic fidelity, and ethical considerations, increasing the credibility of the resource.
Weaknesses: The annotation quality of real infographics is only evaluated on a small sample (1,250 images) without inter-annotator agreement, detailed protocol, or per-category breakdown, leaving uncertainty about annotation consistency and quality.

Fine-grained chart-type (75 types) and mark-level (26 categories) annotations are only available for synthetic infographics; real infographics lack these due to model limitations, reducing the dataset's utility for fine-grained real-world detection.

The Thinking-with-Boxes gains are modest (e.g., o4-mini overall from 63.2 to 64.9) and only evaluated on ChartQAPro; no comparison with other visual grounding methods (e.g., Set-of-Marks) or other chart QA benchmarks is provided, and the impact of detection/OCR errors is not isolated.
VLM experiments rely solely on proprietary models (o1, o3, o4-mini); no open-source VLM is tested, and no statistical significance tests are reported.

The object detection benchmark is not fully systematic: foundation models are often tested zero-shot with only two class names, few-shot prompting is only tested on a subset, and fine-tuning is limited by GPU memory, making comparisons less comprehensive than claimed.
Text annotations are obtained via PP-OCRv4 without reported accuracy on infographic text, which could affect both dataset quality and the grounded CoT prompts.
Presentation issues include incomplete tables, broken internal references, and inconsistencies (e.g., 67 vs. 75 chart types, unclear definitions of metrics and class names).
Dataset release links are redacted in the anonymized version, and real images are only available via source URLs, which may affect reproducibility if links change or content is removed.
Questions: How were the 1,250 evaluation samples selected, what IoU threshold was used for precision/recall, and what was the inter-annotator agreement among experts?
Are fine-grained chart-type and mark-level annotations available for real infographics, or only for synthetic? If only synthetic, how does this affect the claimed comprehensiveness of the dataset?
What is the accuracy of PP-OCRv4 text annotations on infographics, and how does OCR noise affect the grounded CoT prompt results?
What is the performance of Thinking-with-Boxes when using ground-truth boxes instead of predicted boxes, and what is the individual contribution of text vs. boxes?
How does Thinking-with-Boxes compare with other visual prompting methods (e.g., Set-of-Marks) and on other chart QA benchmarks (ChartQA, PlotQA, InfographicVQA)?
Why does the diversity analysis report 67 chart types while the annotation taxonomy lists 75, and are all 75 present?
Were the modifications to the relaxed accuracy metric consistently applied to all baselines, and could they affect comparability with official ChartQAPro results?
How many expert annotators were involved in the model-in-the-loop refinement, how many rounds were performed, and was the final detector retrained on corrected real labels?
Would more descriptive prompts (e.g., listing specific chart types) improve zero-shot detection performance of foundation models?
Are the dataset and code publicly available, and what are the exact licenses for both real and synthetic infographics?
Limitations: Real infographics are collected from only 10 online platforms, which may introduce domain bias and limit diversity of styles and topics.

Synthetic infographics are derived from 1,072 templates, potentially limiting coverage of novel or composite chart designs; 92.64% CLIP coverage leaves a non-trivial fraction of real infographics unrepresented.
The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline may propagate errors from the initial synthetic-trained model into real annotations, and systematic bias is not thoroughly measured.
Fine-grained annotations are absent for real infographics, restricting the scope of fine-grained detection evaluation.
Text annotations from OCR may contain errors, especially on stylized or overlapping text.
The chart understanding experiments are limited to ChartQAPro and proprietary VLMs, so generalization to open-source models and other benchmarks is unclear.
Releasing only source URLs rather than images may lead to broken links or non-reproducible downloads.
The paper does not provide a standardized benchmark protocol for InfoDet, making comparisons across future methods less consistent.
